Example: Read the alcohol label

Problem. A hand-sanitizer label reads “ethyl alcohol 62%.” A swab packet reads “70% isopropyl alcohol.” A bottle of vodka is labeled 80 proof. (a) Does the sanitizer meet the CDC’s advice? (b) What percent alcohol is the vodka, and could it replace hand sanitizer?

Solution. (a) The CDC advises a hand sanitizer with at least 60% alcohol when soap and water are not available. 62% is above 60%, so yes. The 70% swab is also above 60%; its 30% water helps the alcohol denature bacterial proteins, as described above. (b) Proof is twice the percent: 80 ÷ 2 = 40% ethanol. That is below 60%, so it is too dilute to work as a hand sanitizer.

Check. Going the other way, 62% ethanol would be 124 proof. More alcohol is not always better: pure alcohol evaporates before it can do its job, which is why swabs are 70%, not 100%.

Example 1: Read Rosa’s lipid panel

Problem. Rosa’s panel (Chapter 9 opening page) reports LDL 142 mg/dL, HDL 38 mg/dL and triglycerides 230 mg/dL, but not her total cholesterol. Use the lab formula to find it, then compare each value with the targets in the box above.

Solution. The lab formula is LDL = total cholesterol − HDL − triglycerides/5. First, 230/5 = 46 mg/dL. Rearrange: total cholesterol = LDL + HDL + triglycerides/5 = 142 + 38 + 46 = 226 mg/dL. Compare: total 226 (target below 200, high); LDL 142 (target below 100, high); HDL 38 (below 40, low); triglycerides 230 (target below 150, high).

Check. Put the answer back in the formula: 226 − 38 − 46 = 142 mg/dL, the reported LDL. Labs stop using this formula when triglycerides are above 400 mg/dL, because the triglycerides/5 estimate is no longer reliable.

Example 2: Making ATP from creatine phosphate

Problem. In a sprinting muscle, creatine kinase moves a phosphate from creatine phosphate to ADP. Use the table above to find ΔG°′ for creatine phosphate + ADP → creatine + ATP.

Solution. Add two reactions. Creatine phosphate + H2O → creatine + Pi releases 10.3 kcal/mol (−10.3, from the table). Making ATP is the reverse of ATP hydrolysis, so ADP + Pi → ATP + H2O needs 7.3 kcal/mol (+7.3). Sum: creatine phosphate + ADP → creatine + ATP, ΔG°′ = −10.3 + 7.3 = −3.0 kcal/mol. The negative sign means the reaction is favorable.

Check. This works because creatine phosphate sits above ATP in the table. A compound below ATP cannot make ATP this way: glucose 6-phosphate gives −3.3 + 7.3 = +4.0 kcal/mol, which is unfavorable. (Use 7.3 kcal/mol for ATP, as in Example 1 and the Professor Tip.)

597203.old: Fewer protons pumped means less ATP: 2.5 per NADH, 1.5 per FADH2.
597203.new:
Fewer protons pumped means less ATP: 2.5 per NADH, 1.5 per FADH2.

Proton bookkeeping: where 2.5 and 1.5 come from

  • For each pair of electrons: Complex I moves about 4 H+, Complex III about 4, and Complex IV about 2 (it moves 4 for each O2, which takes two electron pairs).
  • NADH (I, III and IV): 4 + 4 + 2 = about 10 H+. FADH2 (III and IV only): 4 + 2 = about 6 H+.
  • ATP synthase uses about 3 H+ to make one ATP, and about 1 more H+ brings ADP and Pi in as the ATP goes out. That is about 4 H+ per ATP delivered to the cell.
  • NADH: 10 ÷ 4 = 2.5 ATP. FADH2: 6 ÷ 4 = 1.5 ATP.

You do not need to memorize the proton counts. They show where the course values 2.5 and 1.5 come from.

Example: Zaitsev’s rule in a ring

Problem. Predict the major and minor alkenes when 2-methylcyclohexanol is dehydrated with H2SO4 and heat.

Solution. Number the ring so the OH carbon is C1 and the CH3 is on C2. The OH carbon has two ring neighbors. C2 is a CH (one H). C6 is a CH2 (two H atoms). Removing the H from C2 puts the C=C between C1 and C2, next to the methyl; the product is 1-methylcyclohexene, whose C=C carries three carbon groups (two ring carbons and the CH3). Removing an H from C6 puts the C=C on the other side; renumbered so the C=C is C1–C2, this is 3-methylcyclohexene, whose C=C carries only two carbon groups. Zaitsev’s rule: 1-methylcyclohexene is major, 3-methylcyclohexene is minor.

Check. Both products are C7H12, which is 2-methylcyclohexanol (C7H14O) minus H2O. In a ring, the ring carbons count as alkyl groups on the C=C, and the neighbor with fewer hydrogens (C2) gives the major product, just as in the open-chain example.

Example 1: Follow ethylene glycol one step at a time

Problem. Ethylene glycol, HOCH2CH2OH, has two 1° alcohol groups. Use the 1° alcohol pattern from Section 4.5 (alcohol → aldehyde → carboxylic acid) to show how the body turns it into oxalic acid.

Solution. Oxidize one end at a time; each arrow is one [O] step.

  1. HOCH2CH2OH → HOCH2CHO (glycolaldehyde): the first CH2OH becomes an aldehyde.
  2. HOCH2CHO → HOCH2COOH (glycolic acid): that aldehyde becomes a carboxylic acid.
  3. HOCH2COOH → OHC–COOH (glyoxylic acid): the second CH2OH becomes an aldehyde.
  4. OHC–COOH → HOOC–COOH (oxalic acid): the second aldehyde becomes a carboxylic acid.

Check. Each step adds a C–O bond or removes a C–H bond, so each is an oxidation. Both ends follow the same alcohol → aldehyde → acid pattern as ethanol. At body pH the –COOH groups lose H+, so the final product is oxalate, −OOC–COO−, the ion that precipitates with Ca2+. The acids made along the way, especially glycolic acid, cause the metabolic acidosis.

Example 3: Three organic molecules, same two questions

Problem. Is each molecule polar? Can it hydrogen bond with itself? (a) ethanol, CH3CH2OH; (b) diethyl ether, CH3CH2OCH2CH3; (c) hexane, CH3CH2CH2CH2CH2CH3.

Solution. (a) Ethanol has polar C–O and O–H bonds. The oxygen has two bonds and two lone pairs, so it is bent, and the two bond dipoles do not cancel. Polar. It has an H on O, so it can hydrogen bond with itself (Section 1.8).

(b) Diethyl ether has two polar C–O bonds. The oxygen is bent, so they do not cancel. Polar, but less so than ethanol. It has no H on O, so it cannot hydrogen bond with itself; it can only accept a hydrogen bond from water.

(c) Hexane has only C–C and C–H bonds, which are essentially nonpolar. Nonpolar, no hydrogen bonding.

Check. Ask the two questions in order. An oxygen with two lone pairs is always bent, so small molecules with a C–O–C or C–O–H group are polar; a hydrocarbon is not.

Example 2: A pentapeptide in one-letter code

Problem. A peptide is written KGDAF. (a) Name the residues and give the N- and C-terminus. (b) How many peptide bonds does it have? (c) What is its net charge at pH 7.4?

Solution. (a) K = lysine, G = glycine, D = aspartate (aspartic acid), A = alanine, F = phenylalanine: Lys-Gly-Asp-Ala-Phe. Sequences are written N to C, so lysine is the N-terminus and phenylalanine is the C-terminus. (b) Five residues are joined by 4 peptide bonds. (c) Count every charged group at pH 7.4: N-terminal –NH3+ (+1), C-terminal –COO− (−1), lysine side chain (basic, +1), aspartate side chain (acidic, −1). Gly, Ala and Phe have neutral side chains. Net charge = +1 − 1 + 1 − 1 = 0.

Check. Peptide bonds = residues − 1, so 5 − 1 = 4, and complete hydrolysis would use 4 water molecules. The two termini cancel each other, so only the side chains decide the net charge; here one basic (+1) and one acidic (−1) side chain also cancel. With 5 residues it is an oligopeptide.

Example 4: Reading the burrito’s label

Problem. The burrito in “Energy in food” above has 30 g carbohydrate, 8 g protein and 12 g fat (260 Calories). (a) What percent of its Calories come from fat? (b) About how long would Rosa need to walk to use 260 Calories? Assume brisk walking (3.5 mph) burns about 140 Calories per 30 minutes, the CDC estimate for a 154-lb person.

Solution. (a) Fat Calories = 12 g × 9 kcal/g = 108 Calories. Percent from fat = 108 ÷ 260 × 100 ≈ 42%. (b) 140 Calories per 30 minutes is about 4.7 Calories per minute. 260 ÷ 4.7 ≈ 55 minutes of walking. Rosa’s 30-minute evening walk uses about 140 Calories, roughly half the burrito.

Check. Fat is only 12 of the 50 grams, yet it supplies 42% of the Calories, because each gram of fat gives 9 kcal instead of 4. A heavier person burns more per minute and a lighter person less, so the walking time is an estimate.
